# 1.1 Mathematics and Physics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Physics is written in the language of measurement, and a measurement is useless unless it carries a unit and an honest indication of how good it is. This section sets out the three habits that every later calculation depends on: attaching units, converting between them by treating units as algebra, and reporting only the digits a measurement actually justifies.

## SI units

Measurements use **units** for standardisation. A number on its own says nothing — "3.58" is not a length. The unit is what fixes the standard against which the quantity was compared, so that a measurement made by one person means the same thing to another.

## Dimensional analysis

**Dimensional analysis** is the technique of treating units like algebraic quantities so that they cancel during conversions. Because units multiply and divide exactly as symbols do, an unwanted unit can be cancelled by arranging it once on the top and once on the bottom of a fraction.

The tool for doing this is the **conversion factor**: a multiplier equal to 1. It is equal to 1 because the two sides express the same physical quantity, for example

$$1\ \text{kg} = 1000\ \text{g} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{1000\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{kg}} = 1$$

Multiplying by 1 never changes the value of a quantity, only the units it is expressed in. That is precisely why the method is safe.

To convert 1.34 kg to grams, multiply by the conversion factor arranged so that kilograms cancel:

$$1.34\ \text{kg} \times \frac{1000\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{kg}} = 1340\ \text{g}$$

The kilograms cancel top and bottom, leaving grams. If you set the factor up the wrong way round, the units do not cancel — they come out as $\text{kg}^2/\text{g}$, which is visibly nonsense. This is the real value of the method: the units themselves tell you whether you have set the conversion up correctly, before you look at the number.

## Significant digits

**Significant digits** are the valid digits in a measurement. A measurement's significant digits consist of all the digits that were actually measured plus one final estimated digit.

That last estimated digit is what makes the count meaningful. When you read a scale, you can read off the marked divisions with certainty and then estimate one further digit between them. Digits beyond that are not measured at all, so writing them would claim a precision the instrument does not have.

The rule for identifying them begins with the simplest case: **nonzero digits are significant**. So 3.58 cm has three significant digits — the 3 and the 5 were read from the scale, and the 8 was estimated.

## Arithmetic with significant digits

Calculations cannot manufacture precision. A result is only as good as the worst measurement that went into it, and the two arithmetic rules are different because addition and multiplication degrade precision in different ways.

| Operation | Rule |
|---|---|
| Addition / subtraction | Round the answer to the least precise **decimal place** among the measurements |
| Multiplication / division | Round the answer to the smallest **number of significant digits** among the measurements |

For addition and subtraction the decimal place matters, because the answer's uncertainty sits in whichever column is first unknown. Adding 1.45 m and 0.032 m gives 1.482 m arithmetically, but 1.45 m is only known to the hundredths place, so nothing beyond the hundredths column is trustworthy and the answer is rounded to 1.48 m.

For multiplication and division the count of significant digits matters instead, because the relative uncertainties combine. An answer quoted to two significant digits is being reported as no better than the two-significant-digit measurement that limited it.

## Check your understanding

1. How many metres are in 2.3 km?
2. Add 1.45 m and 0.032 m, rounding appropriately.
3. Multiply 3.4 kg by a second measured quantity, rounding the result for significant digits.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unit** | The standard attached to a measurement so that measurements can be compared; measurements use units for standardisation |
| **Dimensional analysis** | Treating units like algebraic quantities so that they cancel during conversions |
| **Conversion factor** | A multiplier equal to 1, such as $1\ \text{kg} = 1000\ \text{g}$, used to change units without changing the quantity |
| **Significant digits** | The valid digits in a measurement: the measured digits plus one estimated digit |

# 1.2 Measurement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A measurement is never a single exact number. It is a comparison, and every comparison carries a margin. This section is about how to report that margin, how to decide whether two measurements actually disagree, and why being precise and being accurate are not the same thing.

## Comparing results

A **measurement** is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard. Nothing is measured in isolation; a length is measured against a metre, a mass against a kilogram. What comes out of that comparison is a value together with a statement of how far the true value might lie from it.

That margin is the **absolute uncertainty**, and it is written to **one significant figure**. A measurement is therefore represented as a value plus or minus its uncertainty, and the uncertainty is quoted with a single digit because there is no sense in claiming to know the size of your doubt to two decimal places.

**Reproducibility** follows directly from this way of writing measurements: two measurements agree if their uncertainties overlap. This is the test to apply whenever a question asks whether two results are consistent. If the ranges implied by the two uncertainties share any values in common, the measurements are in agreement — the difference between them is no larger than the doubt you already admitted to. If the ranges do not overlap at all, the measurements genuinely disagree, and something other than ordinary measurement error is responsible.

## Propagation of uncertainties

Uncertainties do not disappear when measurements are combined; they carry through into the result. For **addition and subtraction**, the uncertainties are combined directly — the uncertainty of the sum or difference is the sum of the individual uncertainties.

Notice that this holds for subtraction as well as addition. Subtracting two measurements does not cancel their uncertainties against each other; it adds them, because either measurement could be off in either direction. This is why a small difference between two large measurements is such an unreliable quantity.

## Precision and accuracy

These two words are used interchangeably in ordinary speech and mean different things in physics.

| | Meaning | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **Precision** | The degree of exactness of a measurement | The instrument used, and reproducibility |
| **Accuracy** | The agreement of a measurement with the true or standard value | Whether the measurement is systematically off |

More significant digits means greater precision. A measurement written with more valid digits is a finer comparison, and that fineness comes from the instrument: a better instrument resolves smaller divisions, so it supports more significant digits.

Accuracy is a separate question entirely. An instrument can be extremely precise and still be wrong — reading consistently to many digits, and consistently off the true value. Precision tells you how tightly repeated measurements cluster; accuracy tells you whether that cluster sits where it should.

## Techniques for accurate measurement

**Parallax error** is the most common practical threat to accuracy when reading a scale. It arises when the eye is positioned off to one side, so that the pointer or meniscus appears to line up against a different part of the scale than it truly does. Avoid it by positioning the eye directly above the scale when taking the reading.

## Check your understanding

1. Compare two given measurements. Are they in agreement?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Measurement** | A comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard |
| **Absolute uncertainty** | The margin quoted with a measurement, written to one significant figure |
| **Reproducibility** | The condition in which measurements agree because their uncertainties overlap |
| **Precision** | The degree of exactness of a measurement; depends on the instrument and on reproducibility, with more significant digits meaning greater precision |
| **Accuracy** | The agreement of a measurement with the true or standard value |
| **Parallax error** | A reading error avoided by positioning the eye directly above the scale |

# 1.3 Graphing Data

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A graph turns a table of numbers into a relationship you can see, and once the relationship is identified it can be written as an equation and used to predict values that were never measured. This section covers how to build a graph properly and how to recognise the three relationships you are expected to know.

## Identifying variables

The **independent variable** is the factor that is changed or manipulated during an experiment. It is the quantity the experimenter controls, and everything else in the graph is arranged around it.

## Drawing a graph

The steps below are in the order they should be carried out.

**Choose a simple scale.** Use a scale that avoids awkward numbers — for instance one large square representing 1 N or 2 N. A scale in units of 3 or 7 makes every point a small arithmetic problem, and errors follow.

**Label the axes.** The independent variable goes on the x-axis, the horizontal one. This convention is what makes graphs comparable between experiments: a reader can look at any correctly drawn graph and know immediately which quantity was controlled.

**Plot the data.** Mark at least five data points, using an X to mark each one. An X marks a position exactly, because the crossing point is unambiguous; a dot spreads out and hides where the reading actually fell.

**Draw the line or curve.** If the points form a straight line, draw the **best-fit line** — a single straight line drawn through the trend of the points rather than a zig-zag joining them. The scatter of points around it is measurement error, and the line is the estimate of the underlying relationship.

## Anomalous points

If a point lies far from the line, check the measurement again. Such a point is an **anomalous point**, and you may choose to ignore it.

The order here matters: re-check first, discard second. An anomalous point can be a mis-recorded reading, in which case checking recovers the true value, and it is only after that check fails that ignoring the point is justified.

## Types of graphs

| Relationship | Form | Shape and behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear** | $y = mx + b$ | Straight line; $m$ is the slope, $b$ is the y-intercept |
| **Quadratic** | Nonlinear | Rises more quickly as $x$ increases |
| **Inverse** | Nonlinear | A hyperbola; $y$ decreases as $x$ increases |

A **linear relationship** is represented by $y = mx + b$, where $m$ is the slope and $b$ is the y-intercept. The slope is calculated from the change in $y$ over the change in $x$:

$$m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$

The slope may be positive, negative, or zero, depending on the relationship. A zero slope means $y$ does not change as the independent variable is changed — the two quantities are unrelated over the range tested.

A **quadratic relationship** is nonlinear, and its distinguishing feature is that the curve rises more quickly as $x$ increases. Equal increases in $x$ produce ever larger increases in $y$.

An **inverse relationship** is also nonlinear, and its graph is a hyperbola: $y$ decreases as $x$ increases. The curve falls steeply at first and then flattens without ever reaching zero.

## Predicting values from a graph

Once the relationship is drawn, the graph becomes a prediction tool. Consider a spring loaded with different weights, where $x$ is the weight in grams and $y$ is the length of the spring in centimetres. To find the length when the weight is 20 g, either read the value off the graph at $x = 20$, or use the equation of the line to estimate it.

Reading from the line rather than from the nearest data point is the whole point of drawing a best-fit line: the line averages out the scatter, so a value taken from it is more trustworthy than any single reading.

## Check your understanding

1. What is the independent variable in an experiment where you measure the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Independent variable** | The factor that is changed or manipulated during an experiment; plotted on the x-axis |
| **Best-fit line** | The straight line drawn through the trend of the plotted points when they form a straight line |
| **Anomalous point** | A point far from the line; check the measurement again, and you may choose to ignore it |
| **Linear relationship** | A relationship represented by $y = mx + b$, with slope $m$ and y-intercept $b$ |
| **Slope** | The change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$; may be positive, negative, or zero |
| **Quadratic relationship** | A nonlinear relationship that rises more quickly as $x$ increases |
| **Inverse relationship** | A nonlinear relationship whose graph is a hyperbola, in which $y$ decreases as $x$ increases |

# 2.1 Picturing Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Before motion can be calculated it has to be defined, and the definition turns out to depend on what you are comparing the object against. This section establishes what it means for something to be in motion and introduces the two diagrams used to picture it.

## What motion means

An object is **in motion** if it changes position relative to another object.

The phrase "relative to another object" is doing the real work in that definition. There is no such thing as moving in an absolute sense; there is only moving with respect to something else. A passenger sitting still in a train carriage is not in motion relative to the carriage, and is in motion relative to the platform. Both statements are correct, and they are not in conflict, because they use different comparisons.

The object used for that comparison is the **reference point**, also called the **frame of reference**: a place or object used for comparison to determine if something is in motion. Choosing the reference point is the first step in describing any motion, because until it is chosen the question "is it moving?" has no answer.

## Motion diagrams

A **motion diagram** is a series of images showing the positions of an object at equal time intervals.

The equal time intervals are essential to the idea. Because the images are separated by the same amount of time each step, the spacing between successive positions is a direct picture of how far the object travelled in each of those equal intervals. Wide gaps mean the object covered more ground per interval; narrow gaps mean it covered less.

This is why the diagram is useful: it helps visualise displacement and velocity. Displacement shows up as the change in position from one image to the next, and velocity shows up in the spacing, since equal times mean the spacing is proportional to the speed.

## The particle model

A **particle model** is a simplified motion diagram in which the object is replaced by single points.

The simplification is legitimate only under a specific condition: the object's size must be much less than the distance it moves. When that holds, the difference between one part of the object and another is negligible compared with the distance travelled, so nothing is lost by shrinking the whole object to a point. When it does not hold — an object that moves only a fraction of its own length — the model breaks down, because different parts of the object are then at meaningfully different places.

In practice, imagine the object as a very small point located at its centre. The motion diagram then becomes a row of dots, and the spacing between those dots carries all the information about how the object moved.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Motion** | An object is in motion if it changes position relative to another object |
| **Reference point (frame of reference)** | A place or object used for comparison to determine if something is in motion |
| **Motion diagram** | A series of images showing the positions of an object at equal time intervals |
| **Particle model** | A simplified motion diagram in which the object is replaced by single points; valid when the object's size is much less than the distance it moves |

# 2.2 When and Where

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Saying where something is requires a system for locating it, and saying how far it moved requires care about whether direction is part of the answer. This section sets up the coordinate system, distinguishes scalars from vectors, and separates three quantities that are often confused: position, distance, and displacement.

## Coordinate systems

A **coordinate system** is defined by two choices: the location of the zero point, and the direction of increasing values.

Both choices are free, and both must be made before any position can be stated. The zero point fixes where "zero" is, and the direction of increase fixes which way is positive. Once made, these choices must be kept for the whole problem — a position of $-3$ m means something only in relation to the origin and positive direction you selected.

## Scalars and vectors

| | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Scalar** | A quantity with magnitude only | Distance, time |
| **Vector** | A quantity with magnitude and direction | Position |

Vectors are represented by arrows. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude and the way it points represents the direction, which means an arrow carries both pieces of information in a single mark on the page.

## Adding and subtracting vectors

Vectors cannot simply be added as numbers, because their directions matter. The graphical method is to move the second vector's tail to the first vector's tip. The vectors are then laid head to tail, and the result runs from the start of the first to the end of the last.

Placing the tail of one arrow at the tip of the other is what makes the operation correct: it represents carrying out the first displacement and then, from wherever that leaves you, carrying out the second.

## Position, distance, and displacement

**Position** is an arrow drawn from the origin to the object, so position is a vector. Its magnitude is how far from the origin the object is and its direction is which way from the origin it lies.

The important distinction in this group is which quantities have direction. Position and displacement have direction; distance does not. Distance is a scalar — it is a magnitude only, a bare number of metres with no sense of which way. Displacement is a vector, so a displacement of 5 m east is a different quantity from a displacement of 5 m west, even though both correspond to a distance of 5 m.

This is why a journey out and back can cover a large distance while producing zero displacement: the distance accumulates regardless of direction, while the displacement is the net change in position and the two directions cancel.

## Time intervals

A **time interval** is the difference between two times. Its SI unit is the second.

Because it is a difference, a time interval does not depend on where the clock's zero was set — the same way a displacement does not depend on where the coordinate origin was placed. Both are changes, and a change is unaffected by the choice of starting reference.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Coordinate system** | A system defined by the zero point location and the direction of increasing values |
| **Scalar** | A quantity with magnitude only, such as distance or time |
| **Vector** | A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as position; represented by arrows |
| **Position** | An arrow from the origin to the object; a vector |
| **Distance** | A scalar quantity of how far an object has travelled, without direction |
| **Displacement** | The change in position; a vector, so it has direction |
| **Time interval** | The difference between two times; SI unit the second |

# 2.3 Position-Time Graphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A motion diagram shows where an object was at each moment; a position-time graph puts the same information onto axes, where it can be read quantitatively. This section establishes the convention for drawing one and what its shape tells you.

## Setting up the axes

On a **position-time graph**, time is placed on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis.

This follows the general graphing convention rather than being a special rule. Time is the quantity that runs on independently of the object, so it takes the horizontal axis, and position — the quantity that responds — takes the vertical.

## Reading the graph

Every point on the curve pairs a time with the position the object occupied at that time. Reading vertically upward from a value on the time axis gives the object's position at that instant; reading horizontally across from a value on the position axis gives the time or times at which the object was there.

Because position is plotted, the vertical change between two points is the change in position over the interval between them. That change in position, divided by the time interval it took, is what the steepness of the graph expresses. A steeper slope means a greater change in position in the same time.

This makes the shape of the line immediately informative. A line rising steeply is an object changing position rapidly; a shallow line is an object changing position slowly; a horizontal line is an object whose position is not changing at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Position-time graph** | A graph with time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis |

# 2.4 How Fast

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

"How fast" turns out to be four different questions, depending on whether direction is included and whether you mean over a whole journey or at a single instant. This section separates velocity from speed and average from instantaneous.

## Average velocity

**Average velocity** is the change in position divided by the time interval over which that change occurred:

$$\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}$$

Because it is built from the change in position, average velocity is a vector: it inherits the direction of the displacement.

On a position-time graph, this quantity is the slope of the line, which is why a steeper slope means a greater change in position over the same interval, and therefore a greater average velocity. Reading a velocity off a position-time graph is simply reading its steepness.

## Speed

**Speed** is the distance travelled per unit of time. Where velocity is built from displacement, speed is built from distance, and distance is a scalar. Speed therefore has magnitude only — it tells you how fast without telling you which way.

**Average speed** is the total distance divided by the total time:

$$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$$

The word *total* is what distinguishes it from average velocity. Average speed accumulates every metre travelled, in whatever direction; average velocity uses only the net change in position. For a journey that returns to its starting point the average velocity is zero, because the displacement is zero, while the average speed is not, because distance was still covered.

## Instantaneous velocity

**Instantaneous velocity** is the velocity at a specific instant, rather than over an interval.

An average tells you what the motion amounted to across a stretch of time and says nothing about what happened within it. A journey with an average velocity of 10 m/s might have been steady throughout, or might have involved stopping and sprinting. Instantaneous velocity is the value at one particular moment — what a speedometer with a direction attached would read.

## Average velocity on motion diagrams

Motion diagrams show both the direction and the magnitude of average velocity. The direction is given by which way the successive positions progress along the diagram, and the magnitude is given by the spacing between them: because the images are separated by equal time intervals, wider spacing means a greater change in position per interval, and therefore a larger average velocity.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Average velocity** | The change in position divided by the time interval; shown by the slope of a position-time graph, where a steeper slope means a greater change in position |
| **Speed** | The distance travelled per unit of time |
| **Average speed** | Total distance divided by total time |
| **Instantaneous velocity** | The velocity at a specific instant |

# 3.1 Acceleration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Velocity describes how position is changing; acceleration describes how velocity is changing. Introducing it means moving up one level of description, and it also means a second family of graphs to read.

## Different kinds of motion

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Uniform motion** | The object moves in a straight line with constant velocity |
| **Nonuniform motion** | The velocity changes along a straight line |

The dividing line between the two is whether velocity stays the same. In uniform motion the velocity never changes, so there is no acceleration at all. In nonuniform motion the velocity changes as the object moves along its straight-line path, and it is that change which acceleration measures.

## Calculating acceleration

Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval over which the change happened:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$

Because a velocity is divided by a time, the unit of acceleration is always a velocity unit divided by a time unit. The SI form is m/s², but m/s/hr, km/hr² and other combinations are equally valid units of acceleration — each is still "how much the velocity changed" over "how long it took".

## Velocity-time graphs

Acceleration is read off a **velocity-time graph** in the same way that velocity is read off a position-time graph: from the slope. The slope of a position-time graph ($d$–$t$) represents average velocity, and by the same reasoning the slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration, because in each case the slope is the change in the plotted quantity divided by the time taken.

This gives the characteristics of the graph directly:

- A **rising line** means velocity is increasing, so the acceleration is positive.
- A **descending line** means velocity is decreasing, so the acceleration is negative.
- A **steeper slope** means a larger acceleration, because the same change in velocity is being achieved in less time.

## Acceleration on motion diagrams

Acceleration can be displayed on a motion diagram using average acceleration vectors, which show how the velocity is changing. Where the velocity vectors on the diagram show the motion itself, the acceleration vectors show the change from one velocity vector to the next — so they point in the direction the velocity is being pushed, not necessarily in the direction the object is travelling.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniform motion** | Motion in which an object moves in a straight line with constant velocity |
| **Nonuniform motion** | Motion in which velocity changes along a straight line |
| **Acceleration** | The change in velocity divided by the time interval; units m/s², m/s/hr, km/hr² and similar |
| **Velocity-time graph** | A graph of velocity against time, whose slope represents acceleration |

# 3.2 Motion with Constant Acceleration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

When the acceleration does not change, the motion can be described completely by a small set of equations, and the velocity-time graph becomes a tool for extracting displacement as well as acceleration.

## Position with constant acceleration

Under constant acceleration, position increases with equal time intervals — but not by equal amounts. Because the velocity itself is growing throughout, each successive equal interval of time is covered at a higher speed than the one before, so each interval adds more to the position than the last.

This is the signature of constant acceleration on a motion diagram: the dots spread further apart as the motion progresses, even though the time between them is unchanged. On a position-time graph it appears as a curve that steepens, since the slope of that graph is the velocity and the velocity is rising.

The equations of motion that follow from constant acceleration are:

$$v_f = v_i + a\,\Delta t$$

$$d_f = d_i + v_i\,\Delta t + \tfrac{1}{2}a\,(\Delta t)^2$$

$$v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2a\,(d_f - d_i)$$

The displacement equation contains a term in $(\Delta t)^2$, which is the mathematical statement of what the motion diagram shows: displacement grows faster than time does.

## Area under a velocity-time graph

The area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis gives the displacement over that interval. Multiplying a velocity by a time gives a displacement, and that product is exactly what an area on these axes represents.

## Positive and negative areas

The sign of the area matters, and it is a common source of error. Area below the $v = 0$ line means negative displacement.

The reason is that a negative velocity means the object is moving in the negative direction, so every interval spent below the axis moves the object backwards. When a graph has area both above and below the axis, the two contributions have opposite signs and partly cancel — which is what makes the net displacement smaller than the total distance travelled.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Position with constant acceleration** | Position increases with equal time intervals, by a greater amount in each successive interval |
| **Negative area** | Area below the $v = 0$ line on a velocity-time graph, representing negative displacement |

# 3.3 Free Fall

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Free fall is the most important special case of constant acceleration, because near Earth's surface the acceleration is fixed at a single known value. Everything from the previous section applies unchanged; only the value of $a$ is now given to you.

## Acceleration due to gravity

The **acceleration due to gravity**, written $g$, has an average value at Earth's surface of

$$g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2 \quad \text{directed downward}$$

The direction is part of the answer, not an afterthought. Acceleration is a vector, and $g$ always points downward regardless of which way the object happens to be travelling at the time.

## What counts as free fall

**Free fall** is motion in which air resistance is negligible and only gravity acts on the object.

The condition is what makes the problem solvable. Objects falling through air experience **air resistance**, which is a form of fluid friction. That is a second force, and once a second force is present the net force is no longer simply gravity and the acceleration is no longer simply $g$. Declaring air resistance negligible is what leaves gravity as the only force, and therefore what fixes the acceleration at $g$ for the whole motion.

## Objects dropped from rest

For an object released from rest, the initial velocity is zero and the equations of motion reduce accordingly. With $a = g$ and $v_i = 0$:

$$d = \tfrac{1}{2}g\,(\Delta t)^2 \qquad v_f = g\,\Delta t$$

The displacement grows with the square of the time, while the final velocity grows in direct proportion to it. This is why the second second of a fall covers so much more ground than the first: the object enters it already moving.

## Objects launched upward

For upward motion, the initial velocity must be non-zero and directed upward. An object cannot rise unless it was given an upward velocity to begin with — gravity supplies no upward push of its own.

Once launched, the velocity changes as follows. During the upward part of the motion the velocity decreases, reaching zero at maximum height. That zero velocity is the definition of the highest point: it is the instant at which the object stops rising and has not yet begun to descend.

The acceleration does not become zero there. It remains $g$, downward, throughout the flight — which is exactly why the velocity keeps decreasing through zero and becomes negative as the object falls back. Treating the top of the flight as a point where "nothing is happening" is the standard error; nothing is happening to the *velocity's magnitude* only for an instant, while the acceleration continues unchanged.

Because the acceleration is constant for the entire flight, the whole journey up and down can be handled as one constant-acceleration problem rather than two.

## Check your understanding

1. What is the magnitude and direction of the acceleration for an object in free fall near Earth's surface?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Acceleration due to gravity ($g$)** | The acceleration of a freely falling object, with an average value of $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ downward at Earth's surface |
| **Free fall** | Motion in which air resistance is negligible and only gravity acts on the object |
| **Air resistance** | The fluid friction experienced by objects falling through air |

# 4.1 Force and Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Kinematics describes motion without asking what caused it. Dynamics asks the causal question, and the answer is force. This section defines force, sets out how to draw it, and states the three laws that connect force to motion.

## What a force is

A **force** is a push or pull on an object that can change the object's velocity or cause deformation.

Both outcomes matter. A force may set an object moving, slow it, or turn it — all changes of velocity — or it may leave the motion alone and change the object's shape instead.

| | |
|---|---|
| Symbol | $F$ |
| Unit | newton (N), equivalently $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$ |

The alternative form of the unit is not a coincidence. A newton is defined as whatever force gives one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared, so the unit itself encodes $F = ma$.

## Systems and force representation

The **system** is the object receiving the force. Identifying the system before anything else is what keeps a force problem straight, because a force only means something once you have said what it acts *on*.

Force is a vector, so it is represented by arrows in diagrams. The arrow's length gives the magnitude and its direction gives the direction of the push or pull.

A **free body diagram (FBD)** is the standard way of drawing this. Draw a particle at the centre of mass of the system, then draw every force acting on that system as an arrow starting from the particle. Reducing the object to a single point is the particle model again: it strips away the object's shape so that only the forces remain.

The discipline of an FBD is that it shows forces acting *on* the system and nothing else. Forces the system exerts on other things belong on those other things' diagrams.

## Types of forces

**Contact forces** result from physical contact between objects — one surface pressing on another, a rope pulling, a hand pushing.

**Field forces** act without contact. Gravity is the example: it is the force of attraction between Earth and an object, and it acts across the gap between them with nothing in between.

## Gravity and weight

**Gravity** is a field force that depends on the gravitational pull between two masses. Its magnitude is

$$F_g = mg \qquad (g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2 \text{ on Earth})$$

and its direction is downward, toward Earth.

Because $g$ appears in the formula, the same mass produces a different gravitational force wherever $g$ differs. Mass is a property of the object; the force of gravity on it is not.

## Combining forces in one direction

The **net force** $F_{\text{net}}$ is the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object. When all the forces lie along one line, the vector sum reduces to simple arithmetic with signs:

| Case | Net force |
|---|---|
| Forces in the same direction | $F_{\text{net}} = F_1 + F_2$ |
| Forces in opposite directions | $F_{\text{net}} = F_1 - F_2$ |

Everything about the object's acceleration depends on this single combined quantity, not on the individual forces. Two large forces in opposition produce the same motion as no forces at all.

## Newton's laws of motion

**Newton's first law (the law of inertia)**: an object remains at rest or in constant motion unless acted upon by a net external force.

The law says that motion needs no cause — only *change* of motion does. An object already moving continues moving without anything sustaining it.

**Newton's second law (the law of acceleration)**: the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.

$$F_{\text{net}} = ma \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m}$$

The units in this relationship are kilograms for mass, newtons for force, and m/s² for acceleration. The two proportionalities are what the equation encodes: doubling the net force doubles the acceleration, while doubling the mass halves it.

The second law also contains the first as a special case. If the net force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and an object with zero acceleration is either at rest or moving with constant velocity.

**Newton's third law (the law of action-reaction pairs)**: if object A exerts a force on object B, then object B exerts an equal but opposite force on object A.

## Check your understanding

1. A 50.0 kg bucket is being lifted by a rope. The rope will not break if the tension is 525 N or less. The bucket started at rest, and after being lifted 3.0 m it is moving at 3.0 m/s. If the acceleration is constant, is the rope in danger of breaking?
2. You are helping to repair a roof by loading equipment into a bucket that workers hoist to the rooftop. If the rope is guaranteed not to break as long as the tension does not exceed 450 N, and you fill the bucket until it has a mass of 42 kg, what is the greatest acceleration the workers can give the bucket as they pull it to the roof?
3. Diego and Mika are trying to fix a tyre on Diego's car, but they are having trouble getting the tyre loose. When they pull together, Mika with a force of 23 N and Diego with a force of 31 N, they just barely get the tyre to budge. What is the magnitude of the force between the tyre and the wheel?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Force** | A push or pull on an object that can change the object's velocity or cause deformation; symbol $F$, unit the newton (N) or $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$ |
| **System** | The object receiving the force |
| **Free body diagram (FBD)** | A diagram in which a particle is drawn at the centre of mass and every force acting on the system is drawn as an arrow |
| **Contact force** | A force resulting from physical contact between objects |
| **Gravity** | A field force depending on the gravitational pull between two masses; the force of attraction between Earth and an object, of magnitude $F_g = mg$ directed downward |
| **Net force ($F_{\text{net}}$)** | The vector sum of all forces acting on an object |
| **Newton's first law (law of inertia)** | An object remains at rest or in constant motion unless acted upon by a net external force |
| **Newton's second law (law of acceleration)** | The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass |
| **Newton's third law (law of action-reaction pairs)** | If object A exerts a force on object B, then object B exerts an equal but opposite force on object A |

# 4.2 Using Newton's Laws

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Newton's laws become useful when they are applied to situations where the answer is not obvious: what a scale really reads, why you feel heavier in a lift, and why a falling object eventually stops speeding up.

## Scales

A scale measures **weight** ($mg$), not mass ($m$).

This is the crucial distinction, and it explains a result that otherwise looks strange. The scale responds to the force pressing on it, and that force is the gravitational force $mg$. On Earth the scale can be calibrated to divide by $g$ and display a mass, which is why bathroom scales appear to read kilograms:

$$F_{\text{scale}} = mg$$

On other planets, scales give different readings, because the gravitational acceleration is different. The mass sitting on the scale has not changed at all — mass is a property of the object — but the force it presses down with has, and the force is what the scale actually senses. A scale calibrated for Earth carried to a planet with a different $g$ will therefore display the wrong mass.

## Apparent weight

**Apparent weight** is the force exerted by the scale on the object standing on it. It is what you *feel* as your weight, and it agrees with $mg$ only when there is no acceleration.

| Situation | Scale reading | Sensation |
|---|---|---|
| Equilibrium (no acceleration) | $F_{\text{scale}} = mg$ | Normal |
| Accelerating upward | $F_{\text{scale}} = m(g + a)$ | Overweight |
| Accelerating downward | $F_{\text{scale}} = m(g - a)$ | Underweight |
| Free fall ($a = g$) | $F_{\text{scale}} = 0$ | Weightlessness |

The pattern follows from Newton's second law applied to the person. The two forces on them are gravity downward and the scale's push upward, and the net of those two must equal $ma$. To accelerate someone upward, the scale must push harder than gravity pulls, so it reads more than $mg$. To let them accelerate downward, it must push less.

**Weightlessness** is the limiting case of this and is the most misunderstood entry in the table. In free fall the acceleration is $g$ itself, so the scale needs to supply no force at all and reads zero. Gravity has not switched off — it is the only force acting, and it is what produces the acceleration. What has vanished is the contact force, and the contact force is what sensation of weight actually consists of.

## Drag force

A **drag force** resists the motion of an object through a fluid, such as air or water. It depends on three things:

- the **motion of the object** — specifically its velocity;
- the **properties of the object**, such as its size and shape;
- the **properties of the fluid**, such as its viscosity and temperature.

The essential behaviour is that drag force increases as velocity increases. Unlike gravity, which is fixed for a given object, drag is not a constant — it grows as the object speeds up. Everything about terminal velocity follows from that one fact.

## Terminal velocity

Consider an object released into a fluid. Initially it is moving slowly, so the drag force is small, gravity dominates, and the object accelerates downward.

As it accelerates, its velocity rises, and because drag increases with velocity the retarding force grows. The net downward force is therefore shrinking, so the acceleration is shrinking too — the object is still speeding up, but less and less rapidly.

Eventually the drag force grows large enough to balance gravity. At that moment the net force is zero, so by Newton's second law the acceleration is zero, and the object stops speeding up. It continues falling at a constant velocity: its **terminal velocity**.

Because drag depends on the size and shape of the object, terminal velocity is not the same for every object — which is exactly why air resistance can be ignored for a dense compact object over a short fall and cannot be ignored for a feather.

## Check your understanding

1. If a bathroom scale reads 50 kg on Earth, what will it read on a planet with a different gravitational acceleration?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Weight** | The gravitational force $mg$ on an object; what a scale measures, as distinct from mass |
| **Apparent weight** | The force exerted by the scale; equal to $mg$ in equilibrium, greater when accelerating upward and less when accelerating downward |
| **Weightlessness** | The condition in free fall, where the scale exerts no force and the apparent weight is zero |
| **Drag force** | A force resisting the motion of an object through a fluid, depending on the object's velocity, the object's size and shape, and the fluid's viscosity and temperature; it increases as velocity increases |
| **Terminal velocity** | The constant velocity reached when the drag force has grown to balance gravity, so that the net force and the acceleration are zero |

# 4.3 Interaction Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Newton's third law is the law students most often quote correctly and apply incorrectly. The reason is almost always the same confusion: mistaking an action-reaction pair for a pair of balanced forces. This section makes the distinction precise.

## Interaction pairs

An **interaction pair**, also called an action-reaction pair of forces, consists of two forces with these properties:

- they act in opposite directions and have equal magnitude;
- they are the same type of force, acting on opposite systems.

Forces always come in pairs. There is no such thing as a single isolated force, because a force is one half of an interaction between two objects — if A pushes B, then B is pushing A. This is Newton's third law, and an action-reaction pair is simply another name for the pair of forces the third law describes.

The phrase "opposite system" is the key to using the law correctly. Each member of the pair acts on a *different* object. The force A exerts on B belongs on B's free body diagram; the force B exerts on A belongs on A's.

## Interaction pairs are not balanced forces

Because the two forces in an interaction pair are equal and opposite, it is tempting to conclude they cancel. They do not, and the reason is that cancelling requires forces to act on the same object.

| | Balanced forces | Interaction pairs |
|---|---|---|
| Act on | The same object | Two different objects |
| Can be added together? | Yes — they sum to $F_{\text{net}} = 0$ | No |
| Type of force | Can be two different kinds of force | Always the same kind of force |
| Effect on motion | Will not change the motion of an object | Might change the motion of an object, if no force can balance them |

Read the table as one argument. Balanced forces act on the same object, so they can be added, and their sum is zero, so the object's motion is unchanged. Interaction pairs act on two different objects, so they cannot be added at all — there is no single object whose net force they contribute to — and each one can perfectly well change the motion of the object it acts on.

Balanced forces also need not be of the same kind: a book on a table is held still by gravity and a normal force, two different kinds of force that happen to balance. The two members of an interaction pair are always the same kind of force as each other, because they are two aspects of a single interaction.

## Check your understanding

1. A suitcase sits on a stationary airport luggage cart. Draw a free body diagram for each object, and specifically indicate any interaction pairs between the two.
2. When a softball with a mass of 0.18 kg is dropped, its acceleration toward Earth is equal to $g$, the acceleration due to gravity. What is the force on Earth due to the ball, and what is Earth's resulting acceleration? Earth's mass is $6.0 \times 10^{24}$ kg.

The second question is the sharpest test of the distinction. The force on Earth is equal in magnitude to the force on the ball, because the two make up an interaction pair — but Earth's acceleration is that force divided by Earth's enormous mass, which is why the ball visibly falls toward Earth and Earth does not visibly rise toward the ball.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Interaction pair (action-reaction pair)** | Two forces of the same type, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, acting on opposite systems; the pair described by Newton's third law |
| **Balanced forces** | Forces acting on the same object which can be added together to give $F_{\text{net}} = 0$, may be of different kinds, and will not change the object's motion |

# 5.1 Vectors

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Vectors were introduced as arrows that carry direction as well as size. Once motion and forces leave a single straight line, that direction has to be handled properly — first graphically, then with trigonometry, and finally by resolving vectors into components, which is the method that scales to any number of vectors at any angles.

## Vectors revisited

A **scalar** is a quantity with only magnitude — mass, speed and time are examples. A **vector** has magnitude and direction.

The **tail-to-tip method** for vector addition is to connect the tail of one vector to the tip of the previous one. The resultant then runs from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last.

## Representing vectors to scale

To represent vectors precisely on paper, choose a scale — for instance 1 cm = 10 m/s — and draw each arrow to that scale.

For a velocity of 40 m/s East using a scale of 1 cm = 10 m/s, the vector is drawn 4 cm long, pointing East. Once a scale is chosen it must be used for every vector in the diagram, because the whole point of a scale drawing is that lengths on the page can be compared and combined as though they were the real quantities.

## Vectors in multiple dimensions

### Graphical solutions

| Method | How it works | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Tail-to-tip** | Place the tail of each vector at the tip of the previous one; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip | When vectors are not along the same line |
| **Parallelogram** | Place the vectors tail-to-tail, construct a parallelogram using them as adjacent sides; the diagonal from the origin is the resultant | For adding two vectors |

The two methods give the same answer, because the parallelogram's opposite sides are equal — sliding one vector along to the tip of the other is exactly what constructs the triangle inside the parallelogram.

### Mathematical solution

For vectors at right angles to each other — one North and one East, say — the resultant can be calculated rather than measured. Its magnitude comes from the Pythagorean theorem:

$$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$$

and its angle is found using trigonometry:

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{B}{A}\right)$$

This works only because the vectors are perpendicular. Perpendicular vectors form a right-angled triangle with their resultant, which is what makes Pythagoras applicable.

## Algebraic addition of vectors

The general method removes the right-angle restriction. **Vector resolution** is the process of breaking a vector into its $x$ and $y$ components:

$$A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

Once every vector has been resolved, the components can be added as ordinary signed numbers, because all the $x$ components lie along one line and all the $y$ components lie along another:

$$R_x = \sum A_x \qquad R_y = \sum A_y$$

The magnitude and direction of the resultant are then recovered from those two totals:

$$R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_y}{R_x}\right)$$

This is why resolution is the method of choice for anything beyond two vectors: it converts an awkward geometric problem into two independent one-dimensional additions, and one-dimensional addition is just arithmetic.

## Check your understanding

1. If $A = 30$ m North and $B = 40$ m South, what is the resultant vector $A + B$?
2. Two forces, one at 60° and one at 120°, act on an object. What is the magnitude and direction of the resultant force?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Scalar** | A quantity with only magnitude, such as mass, speed or time |
| **Tail-to-tip method** | Vector addition performed by connecting the tail of one vector to the tip of the previous one; used when vectors are not along the same line |
| **Parallelogram method** | Vector addition performed by placing vectors tail-to-tail and constructing a parallelogram, where the diagonal from the origin is the resultant |
| **Resultant** | The single vector equivalent to the sum of the vectors being added |
| **Vector resolution** | Breaking a vector into its $x$ and $y$ components so that the components can be added separately |

# 5.2 Friction

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Friction is the force that resists motion between surfaces in contact. It behaves differently depending on whether the surfaces are already sliding, and the difference is not a technicality — it is what makes the two friction equations different in form.

## Factors affecting friction

**Nature of the surfaces.** Rough surfaces create more friction than smooth ones, because they interlock more. The microscopic irregularities of two rough surfaces catch on each other, and sliding requires them to be forced past.

**Normal force.** The greater the **normal force** — the force pushing the surfaces together — the greater the friction. Pressing the surfaces harder together forces those irregularities into deeper contact.

Combining the two: friction increases when surfaces are rougher and when more force is applied to press them together. The first factor is captured by the coefficient of friction, the second by the normal force, and the friction equations are simply the product of the two.

## Static and kinetic friction

| | When it acts | Equation |
|---|---|---|
| **Static friction** ($f_s$) | Two surfaces are not moving relative to each other, but there is a tendency for motion | $f_s \le \mu_s F_N$ |
| **Kinetic friction** ($f_k$) | Two surfaces are sliding past each other | $f_k = \mu_k F_N$ |

Here $\mu_s$ is the **coefficient of static friction**, $\mu_k$ is the **coefficient of kinetic friction**, and $F_N$ is the normal force.

The difference in the two equations is the difference between $\le$ and $=$, and it reflects a genuine difference in behaviour. Kinetic friction has a definite value once sliding begins. Static friction does not have a fixed value; it takes whatever value is needed, up to a limit.

## Measuring friction

Consider pushing an object that is at rest. Static friction will match the applied force, up to a maximum value.

Take a 10 kg box with given coefficients of static and kinetic friction, and work through what happens as the applied force increases:

- **No force applied (0 N):** there is no friction at all, and the object stays at rest. Static friction is a response, not a standing force — with nothing to oppose, it is zero.
- **A small applied force:** static friction rises to match it exactly, so the net force stays zero and the box does not move.
- **Applied force at the maximum:** static friction has reached $\mu_s F_N$ and can rise no further.
- **Applied force beyond the maximum:** static friction cannot balance the push, the box begins to slide, and kinetic friction takes over at the fixed value $\mu_k F_N$.

## Important relationships

Static friction is generally higher than kinetic friction for the same surfaces. The two equations to use are:

$$f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s F_N \qquad \qquad f_k = \mu_k F_N$$

Because $\mu_s > \mu_k$ for the same pair of surfaces, getting an object moving takes more force than keeping it moving. This is the familiar experience of a heavy box that suddenly lurches forward once it breaks free: the resisting force drops the instant sliding begins, so the same push that was barely enough to start the motion is now more than enough to accelerate it.

## Check your understanding

1. If you were to increase the normal force acting on an object — for example by pressing down on it — explain how this would affect both static and kinetic friction.
2. A 25 kg box is pushed across a floor with a 49 N force at constant speed. What is the coefficient of friction?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Normal force ($F_N$)** | The force pushing two surfaces together; the greater it is, the greater the friction |
| **Static friction ($f_s$)** | Friction acting when two surfaces are not moving relative to each other but there is a tendency for motion; $f_s \le \mu_s F_N$ |
| **Kinetic friction ($f_k$)** | Friction acting when two surfaces are sliding past each other; $f_k = \mu_k F_N$ |
| **Coefficient of static friction ($\mu_s$)** | The constant relating maximum static friction to the normal force; generally higher than $\mu_k$ for the same surfaces |
| **Coefficient of kinetic friction ($\mu_k$)** | The constant relating kinetic friction to the normal force |

# 5.4 Force and Motion in Two Dimensions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

With vector resolution and friction in place, force problems can be tackled in two dimensions. Two situations recur: an object held in equilibrium by several forces, and an object on an inclined plane where gravity has to be split into components.

## Equilibrium revisited

An object is in **equilibrium** when the net force acting on it is zero. This can happen when the object is at rest, or when it is moving with constant velocity — Newton's first law makes no distinction between the two, because neither involves a change of velocity.

Graphically, equilibrium has a striking signature: if the force vectors form a closed triangle, the net force is zero and the object is in equilibrium. Adding vectors tail-to-tip means the resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip, so if the last tip lands back on the first tail the resultant has zero length.

The **equilibrant** is the force that balances the other forces. It has the same magnitude as the resultant but acts in the opposite direction — which is precisely the condition for the two together to sum to zero.

## Equilibrant force

**For two forces:** the equilibrant is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the force it balances. A force of 1000 N at 15° North of East requires an equilibrant force of 1000 N at 15° South of West to maintain equilibrium — the same size, reversed by 180°.

**For three or more forces:** find the resultant of the first two forces, then continue. The equilibrant is equal in magnitude to the resultant but points in the opposite direction.

The general procedure is therefore always the same: reduce all the applied forces to a single resultant, then reverse it. Finding the equilibrant is never a separate technique — it is vector addition followed by a change of sign.

## Motion along a level surface

For motion at constant speed across a level surface, the applied force equals the friction force. Constant speed means zero acceleration, which means zero net force, which means the push and the friction must be equal and opposite.

If the applied force is then doubled, the object accelerates — and, importantly, friction remains constant. Kinetic friction is $\mu_k F_N$, and neither the coefficient nor the normal force changes when you push harder horizontally. All of the extra force therefore goes into the net force, and hence into acceleration.

## Motion along an inclined plane

On an incline, gravity no longer points along or across the surface, so it must be resolved. The gravitational force splits into two components:

| Component | Direction | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel component | Parallel to the slope | Causes motion down the slope |
| Perpendicular component | Perpendicular to the slope | Affects the normal force |

Separating the two is what makes incline problems tractable. The parallel component is the only part of gravity that drives motion along the surface, so it is the part that appears in the net force along the slope. The perpendicular component is balanced by the surface and determines the normal force — which in turn sets the friction, since friction depends on $F_N$.

This is why an object on a steeper slope both accelerates more and experiences less friction: tilting the slope increases the parallel component and decreases the perpendicular one at the same time.

## Check your understanding

1. If three forces of 10 N, 15 N and 20 N form a closed triangle, is the object in equilibrium?
2. Can 100 N, 150 N and 300 N form an equilibrium? Why?

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equilibrium** | The condition in which the net force acting on an object is zero; the object may be at rest or moving with constant velocity |
| **Equilibrant** | The force that balances the other forces, equal in magnitude to the resultant but opposite in direction |

# 6.1 Projectile Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A projectile follows a curved path, which looks like a hard problem until you notice that the curve is the combination of two simple motions happening at once. Splitting them apart is the entire technique.

## What a projectile is

**Projectile motion** is the motion of an object moving through the air under the influence of gravity alone.

The forces are correspondingly simple: only gravity acts on the projectile, provided air resistance is ignored. Nothing pushes it forward — the forward motion is left over from the launch and continues under Newton's first law because there is no horizontal force to change it.

## Independence of motion

The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of each other:

| Direction | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Horizontal | Constant velocity — there is no horizontal force |
| Vertical | Constant acceleration $g$ downward — gravity acts vertically |

Because gravity acts straight downward, it changes the vertical velocity and leaves the horizontal velocity untouched. The two motions therefore proceed side by side without interfering, and each can be handled with the one-dimensional equations already established. The horizontal motion uses

$$x = v_x t$$

and the vertical motion uses the constant-acceleration equations with $a = g$.

The only quantity the two motions share is the time. That shared time is what links them, and it is why almost every projectile problem is solved by finding the time from one direction and using it in the other.

## Typical problems

### A stone dropped from rest

*A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 8.0 s. Find its velocity and displacement.*

This is pure vertical motion with no horizontal component at all.

1. Find the velocity after 8.0 s using $v_f = gt$.
2. Find the displacement during that time using $d = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.

### A projectile launched horizontally

*A projectile is launched horizontally from a height. Determine its time of flight and range.*

1. **Find the time of flight** from the vertical motion. The projectile was launched horizontally, so its initial vertical velocity is zero and the drop height gives the time directly: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.
2. **Find the horizontal range** using that time in the horizontal equation: $x = v_x t$.

The order is forced by the physics. The height tells you nothing about the horizontal motion and the launch speed tells you nothing about the fall — the time of flight is the only bridge between them. Note what this means: a projectile fired horizontally hits the ground at the same moment as one simply dropped from the same height, because their vertical motions are identical.

### The monkey and hunter problem

*Where should the hunter aim at a monkey that will drop from its branch at the instant the shot is fired?*

The bullet and the monkey experience the same gravitational acceleration. Since both undergo the same vertical displacement in the same time, the hunter should aim directly at the monkey.

The result is counter-intuitive only if you think of the bullet's fall as spoiling the aim. Both objects fall by exactly the same amount, so the fall cancels out of the comparison: whatever height the bullet loses, the monkey has lost the same, and they meet.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Projectile motion** | The motion of an object moving through the air under the influence of gravity alone |
| **Independence of motion** | The principle that the horizontal motion of a projectile (constant velocity) and its vertical motion (constant acceleration) proceed independently, linked only by the shared time |
| **Time of flight** | The time a projectile spends in the air, determined by its vertical motion |
| **Range** | The horizontal distance a projectile travels, found from $x = v_x t$ using the time of flight |

# 6.2 Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

An object going round a circle at constant speed is accelerating, which sounds like a contradiction until you remember that velocity includes direction. The direction is changing continuously, and that change is what circular motion is about.

## Uniform circular motion

**Uniform circular motion (UCM)** is movement at constant speed around a circle.

Three facts define the geometry of the situation:

- The **velocity** is always tangential to the circle. At any instant the object is heading along the tangent — the direction it would carry on in if everything else stopped acting on it.
- The **acceleration** is always directed toward the centre. This is the **centripetal acceleration**.
- The **centripetal force** is the net force required to keep an object moving in a circle.

The acceleration points to the centre rather than along the motion because the speed is not changing — only the direction is. An acceleration component along the velocity would speed the object up or slow it down; a purely perpendicular acceleration turns it without changing its speed, and perpendicular to the tangent is exactly the direction of the centre.

## Formulas

The speed of an object completing one circle of radius $r$ in a period $T$ is the circumference divided by the time:

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

The centripetal acceleration and the centripetal force follow:

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} \qquad\qquad F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

Note that the centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is a requirement — the net inward force that circular motion demands — and in any real problem it has to be supplied by something: a string, friction, gravity. Identifying what is playing that role is the first step in every circular motion problem.

## Typical problems

### Finding the tension in a string

*A stopper is swung in a circle. Find the tension in the string.*

1. Find the velocity using the period equation, $v = 2\pi r / T$.
2. Find the centripetal force from $F_c = mv^2/r$.
3. Since the tension in the string provides the centripetal force, the tension equals that value.

Step 3 is the step that carries the physics. The string is the only thing pulling the stopper inward, so whatever inward force the circular motion requires, the string must be supplying it.

### A car on a curve

*A car moves around a curve. Find its centripetal acceleration and the required friction coefficient.*

1. Find the centripetal acceleration from $a_c = v^2/r$.
2. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction. Here friction is what supplies the centripetal force, so $\mu_s mg = mv^2/r$, giving

$$\mu_s = \frac{v^2}{rg}$$

The mass cancels, so the coefficient needed to hold a curve does not depend on how heavy the car is — only on how fast it is going and how tight the curve is.

### Why a passenger feels pushed outward

*A passenger in a turning car feels pushed outward. Explain why.*

There is no actual outward force. The sensation is an inertial effect, caused by the passenger's resistance to changing motion. The real force involved acts inward: the car applies a friction force inward to keep the passenger moving in a circle.

To set the explanation out properly:

1. **Draw the free body diagram**, showing the forces acting on the passenger.
2. **Identify the real force.** The inward force — friction from the seat, or a push from the door — is what keeps the passenger moving in a circle.
3. **Explain the sensation.** The body wants to continue in a straight line, by Newton's first law, so as the car curves away beneath it the passenger presses against the door, and it feels as though an outward force is acting.

The key point is that the feeling reports the *absence* of a straight-line path, not the presence of an outward force. What the passenger senses is the seat and door pushing them inward off the tangent they would otherwise follow.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniform circular motion (UCM)** | Movement at constant speed around a circle |
| **Centripetal acceleration** | The acceleration of an object in circular motion, always directed toward the centre; $a_c = v^2/r$ |
| **Centripetal force** | The net force required to keep an object moving in a circle; $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Period ($T$)** | The time taken to complete one circle, related to speed by $v = 2\pi r/T$ |

# 7.1 Planetary Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The law of universal gravitation was not guessed at. It was arrived at through two thousand years of argument about what orbits the what, followed by a careful analysis of the best planetary data ever collected. This section follows that path, because the law makes far more sense as the answer to Kepler's puzzle than as a formula on its own.

## Models of planetary motion

### Geocentrism

**Geocentrism** is the model in which Earth is the centre of the universe. It held from roughly 400 BC to 1600 AD, and its early supporters included **Aristotle** and **Zhang Heng**.

**Ptolemy's model** was the developed form of geocentrism: the Sun and the planets orbited Earth. Its difficulty was that planets do not move steadily across the sky — they slow, stop and briefly reverse. Ptolemy accounted for this irregular motion using **epicycles**, spinning wheels carrying the planets around smaller circles as those circles were carried around Earth.

**Tycho Brahe** built instruments that measured the positions of planets and stars accurately, and proposed a hybrid model: the Sun and Moon orbit Earth, while the other planets orbit the Sun. His lasting contribution was the data rather than the model.

### Heliocentrism

**Heliocentrism** places the Sun at the centre: the Moon revolves around Earth, while Earth and the other planets revolve around the Sun.

**Nicolaus Copernicus** revived the proposal that the planets revolve around the Sun. The guide prints that he was the first human to propose it; that is an error — heliocentrism was already proposed in antiquity, and Copernicus reintroduced it.

**Johannes Kepler** discovered the laws that describe the motion of every planet, by analysing Brahe's data. This is the point at which accurate measurement produced a genuinely new result: Brahe measured, Kepler analysed, and the laws that emerged were far simpler than the epicycles they replaced.

## Kepler's laws

**Kepler's first law.** The paths of planets are **ellipses**, with the Sun at one focus. Comets orbit the Sun in ellipses too. The guide adds stars to that list; that is an error — stars do not orbit the Sun, and the law is about the planets.

**Kepler's second law.** An imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. The consequence is that a planet closer to the Sun moves faster, and a planet further away moves more slowly — to sweep the same area with a shorter line, the planet must travel further along its path.

**Kepler's third law.** The square of the ratio of the periods of any two planets is equal to the cube of the ratio of their average distances from the Sun:

$$\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^3$$

where $T_1$ and $T_2$ are the periods of the two planets, and $r_1$ and $r_2$ are their average distances from the Sun.

## The law of universal gravitation

Objects attract other objects with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them:

$$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F$ | The gravitational force between the two objects |
| $G$ | The gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| $m_1, m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the centres of the two objects |

The word **universal** is the substantial claim. The gravitational force acts between any two objects, anywhere in the universe — the same law governs an apple and a galaxy.

## Universal gravitation and Kepler's third law

Newton's law agreed with Kepler's third law, and the agreement is what established it. The derivation runs as follows.

For calculation, assume a planet orbits the Sun in a circular orbit — in reality the orbit is an ellipse, but the circle is a good enough approximation to work with. A planet in a circular orbit is in uniform circular motion, so it requires a centripetal force directed at the Sun, and the universal gravitational force is what provides that centripetal force.

Setting the gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force gives the period of a planet orbiting the Sun:

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$$

Square this and the period comes out proportional to $r^3$, which is exactly Kepler's third law. A law that Kepler had extracted empirically from Brahe's observations fell out of Newton's force law as a consequence.

## Measuring the universal gravitational constant

The constant $G$ was measured by **Cavendish's experiment**, known as "weighing Earth". Having $G$ allowed Cavendish to determine Earth's mass, using the fact that the gravitational force on an object is its mass times the acceleration due to gravity:

$$F_g = mg$$

The mass of Earth is $5.98 \times 10^{24}$ kg.

The experiment is difficult for a reason worth stating plainly. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects, but the force between everyday objects is so small that it cannot be observed. Gravity only becomes conspicuous when one of the masses is astronomically large, which is why it took a specially built apparatus to detect the attraction between laboratory-sized masses at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Geocentrism** | The model in which Earth is the centre of the universe, held from about 400 BC to 1600 AD |
| **Epicycles** | Spinning wheels used in Ptolemy's model to account for the irregular motion of the planets |
| **Heliocentrism** | The model in which the Moon revolves around Earth while Earth and the other planets revolve around the Sun |
| **Kepler's first law** | The paths of planets are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus |
| **Kepler's second law** | An imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals, so a planet closer to the Sun moves faster |
| **Kepler's third law** | The square of the ratio of the periods of any two planets equals the cube of the ratio of their average distances from the Sun |
| **Law of universal gravitation** | Objects attract other objects with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them |
| **Gravitational constant ($G$)** | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| **Cavendish's experiment** | The experiment that measured $G$, also known as "weighing Earth", which allowed Earth's mass to be determined as $5.98 \times 10^{24}$ kg |
