# 5.8 Satellites and "Weightlessness"

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Free fall and apparent weight

**Free fall** is the condition of an object falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance.

**Weightlessness** occurs when an astronaut in orbit feels weightless because both the shuttle and the astronaut are in free fall together. The quotation marks in the section title are doing real work: **the gravitational force is not zero**. There is no apparent weight only because there is no support force — the floor is falling away at exactly the rate the astronaut is falling, so it never pushes back.

What you feel as your weight is in fact the support force from whatever is holding you up. Remove the support while leaving gravity untouched, and the sensation of weight vanishes although the force has not.

## Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit is held there by gravity, and gravity is therefore the source of the centripetal force. Equating the two,

$$\frac{G M m}{r^{2}} = \frac{m v^{2}}{r}$$

gives the **orbital speed**, in which the satellite's own mass has cancelled:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$

where $M$ is the mass of the central object and $r$ the radius of the orbit measured from its centre. The **orbital period** follows from the fact that one lap covers a circumference:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$$

Because the satellite's mass cancels, a heavy satellite and a light one at the same altitude travel at the same speed with the same period — the same cancellation, and the same reason, as for objects in free fall at the surface.

## Worked example

*A satellite orbits Earth 225 km above its surface. The Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and its radius $6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$. What are the satellite's orbital speed and period?*

The orbital radius is measured from the centre of the Earth, so the altitude must be added to the Earth's radius:

$$r = 6.38 \times 10^{6} + 2.25 \times 10^{5} = 6.605 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$$

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(5.97 \times 10^{24})}{6.605 \times 10^{6}}} \approx 7.77 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$$

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi (6.605 \times 10^{6})}{7.77 \times 10^{3}} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{3}\ \text{s}$$

which is about 89 minutes. Forgetting to add the altitude to the Earth's radius is the standard error in this calculation, and it gives an answer that looks plausible, so it is worth checking deliberately.

## Check your understanding

**What causes an object to stay in orbit around Earth?**

Gravity. It supplies the centripetal force that continuously turns the satellite's velocity toward the Earth, so the satellite keeps falling toward the Earth without ever getting closer to it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free fall** | When an object is falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance |
| **Weightlessness** | The sensation experienced when an astronaut and the craft are in free fall together; the gravitational force is not zero, but there is no apparent weight because there is no support force |
| **Orbital speed** | $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, where $M$ is the mass of the central object |
| **Orbital period** | $T = 2\pi r / v$, the time for one complete orbit |

# 5.9 Kepler's Laws and Newton's Synthesis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kepler's laws

Kepler's laws describe how planets actually move, and they were established from observation before there was any theory to explain them.

**First law.** Planets orbit the Sun in **elliptical** paths, with the Sun at one **focus**. Not at the centre — at a focus, which means a planet's distance from the Sun changes over the course of its year.

**Second law.** A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal time intervals**. Since the line is shorter when the planet is nearer the Sun, the planet must travel further along its orbit in a given time to sweep the same area, and so **planets move faster when they are closer to the Sun**. The law is a statement about speed disguised as a statement about area.

## Newton's synthesis

The orbital period and the orbital distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and **Kepler's third law can be derived using Newton's law** of universal gravitation.

The derivation is the same equation used for satellites in the previous section. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for a planet of mass $m$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ about a central object of mass $M$:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

Substituting $v = 2\pi r/T$ and rearranging gives

$$T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}\,r^{3}$$

so $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$, with a constant of proportionality that depends only on the mass of the central object — exactly the two dependencies stated above. Comparing two bodies orbiting the same central object, the constant cancels:

$$\frac{T_1^{2}}{T_2^{2}} = \frac{r_1^{3}}{r_2^{3}}$$

This is the synthesis: a law obtained from astronomical observation is shown to be a consequence of the same force that governs falling objects on Earth. The planets were not obeying a special rule of their own.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following best explains why astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless?**

Because the station and the astronauts are in free fall together, so nothing supports the astronauts and they have no apparent weight. It is not because gravity is absent at that altitude — gravity is what holds the station in orbit.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kepler's first law** | Planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun at one focus |
| **Kepler's second law** | A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals; planets move faster when closer to the Sun |
| **Kepler's third law** | $T^2 \propto r^3$; the orbital period and distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and the relation is derivable from Newton's law of universal gravitation |

# 6.1 Work Done by a Constant Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What work is

**Work** is a scalar: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement.

$$W = F d \cos\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Its unit is the **joule** (J).

The definition has two halves, and both matter. There must be a displacement, and the force must have a component along it. A force at right angles to the motion contributes nothing at all, because $\cos 90° = 0$ — the parallel component it needs to supply is zero.

Work is **positive** when the force and the displacement are in the same direction.

## Worked example

*A sailor pulls a boat a distance of 0.30 m along a dock using a rope that makes a 25.0° angle with the horizontal. How much work does the sailor do on the boat if he exerts a force of 255 N on the rope?*

The boat moves horizontally, but the rope pulls at 25.0° to the horizontal, so only the horizontal component of the 255 N does work:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta = 255 \times 0.30 \times \cos 25.0° \approx 69\ \text{J}$$

The same pattern — pulling a crate with a rope at an angle — recurs throughout the chapter.

## Lifting an object

Lifting an object vertically is the other standard case. Here the force is along the displacement, and the work done equals the change in gravitational potential energy of the object. This is the first sign of the connection developed in the rest of the chapter: work is the mechanism by which energy is transferred and stored.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following results in zero work?**

A. Pushing a box across the floor
B. Holding a book without moving it
C. Pulling a sled in the snow
D. Dropping an object from a height

**Answer: B.** Holding a book takes force, but the book does not move, so the displacement is zero and $W = Fd\cos\theta = 0$. Effort is not work in the physics sense; work requires the point of application to move.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work** | A scalar quantity: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Joule (J)** | The unit of work |
| **Positive work** | Work done when force and displacement are in the same direction |

# 6.2 Work Done by a Varying Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Work as an area

$W = Fd\cos\theta$ assumes a single value of $F$ for the whole displacement. When the force changes with position, there is no single $F$ to put in the formula, and work must be found another way: **from the area under the force versus displacement curve.**

The work done is the area between the graph of $F$ and the $x$-axis, between the starting and finishing positions.

This is not a new definition of work but the same one applied piecewise. Over a displacement small enough that the force barely changes, the work is $F$ times that small displacement — the area of a thin strip under the curve. Adding the strips across the whole journey adds their areas, and the total is the area under the curve. The constant-force case is the special one where the graph is a horizontal line and the area is a rectangle, $F$ times $d$.

## Integration

In the limit of infinitely thin strips, that sum is an integral:

$$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$$

## Check your understanding

**What does the area under a Force versus Position graph represent?**

A. Velocity
B. Acceleration
C. Work
D. Power

**Answer: C.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work done by a varying force** | The area between the force–displacement curve and the $x$-axis, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$ |

# 6.3 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Principle

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kinetic energy

**Kinetic energy** is the energy of motion:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$$

Like work, it is measured in joules, and like work it is a scalar — it carries no direction, so the sign of the velocity is irrelevant. An object moving left at $5\ \text{m/s}$ and one moving right at $5\ \text{m/s}$ have the same kinetic energy.

The dependence on $v^2$ means kinetic energy grows far faster than speed: doubling the speed of an object quadruples its kinetic energy.

## The work-energy principle

The **work-energy principle** states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^{2}$$

This is what makes work worth defining. It converts a question about forces and displacements into a question about speeds, without any of the intermediate detail about how the force varied along the way.

## Worked example

*A 145 g baseball is thrown so that it acquires a speed of 25 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?*

Convert the mass to kilograms first — $145\ \text{g} = 0.145\ \text{kg}$ — since the joule is built on kilograms, metres and seconds:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.145)(25)^{2} \approx 45\ \text{J}$$

## Check your understanding

**If net work on an object is positive, what happens to its kinetic energy?**

A. It decreases
B. It stays the same
C. It becomes zero
D. It increases

**Answer: D.** By the work-energy principle $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$, so positive net work means a positive change in kinetic energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kinetic energy (KE)** | The energy of motion, $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Work-energy principle** | The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy |

# 6.4 Potential Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Stored energy

**Potential energy (PE)** is stored energy due to position. Two forms appear in this chapter:

| Form | Formula | Stored by |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$ | Raising a mass to a height $y$ |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$ | Stretching or compressing a spring by $x$ from its natural length |

Here $k$ is the spring stiffness constant, in newtons per metre.

## The reference point

Potential energy is **relative to a chosen zero level**. There is no absolute height and therefore no absolute gravitational potential energy: you choose where $y = 0$, and every value of $PE$ in the problem is quoted with respect to that choice.

The choice is free, and different choices give different numbers for the *same* physical situation. What they never change is a **difference** in potential energy between two points, and it is always a difference that appears in physical predictions. So choose whatever zero makes the arithmetic easiest — usually the lowest point of the motion, or the starting point — and then use it consistently.

## Worked example: a roller-coaster car

*A 1000 kg roller-coaster car moves from point 1 to point 2 and then to point 3.*

**(a) Taking $y = 0$ at point 1**, the gravitational potential energy at points 2 and 3 is $mgy$ with each height measured from point 1. A point below the chosen zero has a negative height, and therefore a negative potential energy — which is perfectly acceptable, since only differences are physical.

**(b) The change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3** is the difference of the two values found in (a).

**(c) Repeating with $y = 0$ at point 3** gives $PE = 0$ at point 3 by definition, and different numbers at points 1 and 2. But the change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3 comes out the same as in (b). That is the lesson of the example: the reference point moves all the individual values up or down together, and cancels out of every difference.

## Worked example: a spring

*A spring has a spring stiffness constant of 440 N/m. How much must this spring be stretched to store 25 J of potential energy?*

Rearranging $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ for $x$:

$$x = \sqrt{\frac{2\,PE}{k}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 25}{440}} \approx 0.34\ \text{m}$$

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following increases an object's gravitational potential energy?**

A. Lowering it to the ground
B. Compressing a spring
C. Raising it to a higher shelf
D. Sliding it on a level surface

**Answer: C.** Gravitational potential energy is $mgy$, so it increases only when $y$ increases. Compressing a spring stores energy, but elastic potential energy, not gravitational.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Potential energy (PE)** | Stored energy due to position |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$, the energy stored by raising a mass to a height |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, the energy stored by stretching or compressing a spring |
| **Spring stiffness constant ($k$)** | The constant, in N/m, measuring how stiff a spring is |
| **Reference point** | The chosen zero level with respect to which potential energy is measured |

# 6.5 Conservative and Nonconservative Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

A **conservative force** is one for which the work done is **path-independent**: it depends only on the starting and finishing points, not on the route taken between them. Gravity is the standard example.

A **nonconservative force** is one for which the work done **depends on the path**. Friction is the standard example — the longer the route, the more work friction does against the motion, even if the object ends up in the same place.

| | Conservative | Nonconservative |
|---|---|---|
| Work done | Path-independent | Depends on the path |
| Example | Gravity | Friction |
| Potential energy | Can be defined | Cannot be defined |

## Identifying which type a force is

The test is the last row of that table: **if a potential energy can be defined for a force, the force is conservative.**

The reason follows from the previous section. Potential energy is a function of *position* alone — $mgy$ depends on where the object is and nothing else. For such a quantity to describe the work a force does, that work must itself depend only on the positions at the two ends of the journey. A force whose work depends on the route taken cannot be summarised by any function of position, so no potential energy exists for it.

## Mechanical energy and friction

*A box sliding down a ramp with friction loses mechanical energy due to friction.*

This is what the distinction costs in practice. Gravity does work on the box that can be fully accounted for as a change in gravitational potential energy, and recovered if the box goes back up. The work done against friction cannot be recovered: it is not stored anywhere as potential energy, and the mechanical energy of the box is reduced by it.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following is a conservative force?**

A. Friction
B. Tension
C. Gravity
D. Air resistance

**Answer: C.** Gravity has a potential energy, $mgy$, defined for it; friction and air resistance both do path-dependent work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conservative force** | A force whose work is path-independent, such as gravity |
| **Nonconservative force** | A force whose work depends on the path taken, such as friction |

# 8.1 Angular Quantities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Rotation needs its own set of quantities, because every point of a rotating body travels a different distance at a different speed while the body as a whole turns by one definite amount. The angular quantities describe the turning itself.

## Angular position and displacement

**Angular position** $\theta$ is the angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line. Its unit is the **radian** (rad), defined by

$$\theta = \frac{s}{r}$$

where $s$ is the arc length in metres and $r$ the radius in metres. A radian is thus the angle for which the arc length equals the radius; being a ratio of two lengths, it is a pure number, which is why radians can be multiplied into linear quantities without carrying a unit along.

Rotation has a sign convention, as straight-line motion does:

| Direction | Sign |
|---|---|
| Counterclockwise | Positive |
| Clockwise | Negative |

## Converting between degrees and radians

A full turn is $360°$ and also $2\pi$ radians, so the two units are related by $180° = \pi\ \text{rad}$:

$$\text{degrees} \to \text{radians:}\quad \theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\deg} \times \frac{\pi}{180}$$

$$\text{radians} \to \text{degrees:}\quad \theta_{\deg} = \theta_{\text{rad}} \times \frac{180}{\pi}$$

## Angular velocity

**Angular velocity** $\omega$ is the rate of change of angular displacement over time:

$$\omega = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$$

measured in radians per second (rad/s). It takes the same sign convention: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative.

Its properties are read off a graph of angular position against time, exactly as velocity is read off a position–time graph in straight-line motion:

- **Constant $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ against time is a straight line.
- **Changing $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ is curved, and the slope of the tangent at a point gives the instantaneous $\omega$ at that moment.

## Relationship between linear and angular quantities

A point at distance $r$ from the axis moves along an arc of length $s = r\theta$, so dividing by the time taken gives its linear speed:

$$v = r\omega$$

This single relation is the bridge between the two descriptions, and it says something that is easy to get wrong: the angular velocity belongs to the *whole rotating body*, while the linear speed belongs to a *particular point on it* and grows with distance from the axis.

## Check your understanding

**Two points, A and B, are on a rotating disk, with B farther from the centre. Which point has a greater angular velocity? Which has a greater linear velocity? Why?**

The disk is rigid, so both points sweep through the same angle in the same time: their **angular velocities are equal**. But $v = r\omega$, and B has the larger $r$, so **B has the greater linear velocity** — it has a longer circle to travel in the same time.

**Convert 2.5 radians into degrees.**

$$2.5 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 143°$$

**Convert 135° into radians.**

$$135 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 2.36\ \text{rad}$$

**The Earth completes one full rotation in 24 hours. What is its angular velocity in rad/s?**

One full rotation is $2\pi$ rad and 24 hours is $86\,400\ \text{s}$, so

$$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{86\,400} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{rad/s}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angular position ($\theta$)** | The angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line, $\theta = s/r$ |
| **Radian (rad)** | The unit of angular position, defined as the arc length divided by the radius |
| **Arc length ($s$)** | The distance measured along the circular path, in metres |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of change of angular displacement over time, $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t$, in rad/s |
